title: Not two
hook: a proud son home from twelve years of study, and a father holding a lump of clay
carry: not two: one clay under every name

segments.voice: Last week ended with the tiger who thought he was a goat: know yourself free, and you are free. Today begins a week on the great school that grew from that idea. Its name is two words long: not two.
screen: `KNOW YOURSELF FREE, AND YOU ARE FREE.`

segments.voice: A young man named Shvetaketu comes home after twelve years of study, sure he knows everything. His father, Uddalaka, asks one quiet question: did you ask for the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, and the unknown becomes known? The son has no idea what he means. So the father picks up a lump of clay. Know this, he says, and you know every pot, every cup, every lamp ever made from it. The pot is only a name. The truth of it is clay.
screen: `HOME FROM TWELVE YEARS OF STUDY.` → `ONE QUIET QUESTION.` → `KNOW THE CLAY, KNOW EVERY POT.`

segments.voice: That's the Chandogya Upanishad, and the father keeps going: in the beginning there was only being, one without a second. Picture a potter's shelf: a water pot, a cup, a little oil lamp. Different names, different uses, and underneath, one clay. A great teacher named Shankara built a whole school on lines like these, and it's called advaita. Dvaita means twoness; a means not. Advaita: not two. Its teachers are careful not to say one, because one sounds like something you could count. Not-two just refuses the split: between the pot and the clay, between you and the world, between your deepest self, the atman, and Brahman, the one reality. Tradition says Shankara was born in Kaladi, in Kerala, became a monk as a boy, walked the length of India teaching, and died at about thirty-two; scholars debate his dates. Here's where it meets a Hindu home. Many Hindus will tell you, without blinking, that the many gods on a family shrine, Ganesha, Krishna, the Goddess, are many names and forms of one reality. For Advaita: many pots, one clay. So when a friend asks how many gods you have, this is one great Hindu answer. An honest frame for the week: Advaita is one great school of Vedanta. Next week come schools that say the soul and God stay two, forever. Hindus hold each, and i won't rank them.
screen: `ONE CLAY, MANY POTS.` · `A-DVAITA: NOT TWO.` · `SHANKARA OF KALADI.` · `MANY NAMES AND FORMS, ONE REALITY.` · then, large: `NOT TWO.`

segments.voice: Pick up two or three things near you that are made of one stuff: a cup, a ring, a wooden spoon. Say each one's name quietly, then say what it's made of. Notice how the name changes and the stuff doesn't. If there's a picture of a god nearby, or a shrine at home, look at it the same way: a name and a form, and, for Advaita, one reality underneath. If you pray, you can bow to that one reality through the form in front of you; if not, just breathe for a moment with that.
Advaita. Not two: the teaching, tied to Shankara, that the self and Brahman, the one reality, are not different, as pots are not different from clay.
Your line: not two. One clay under every name on the shelf. Two eighty-one, in the books.

screen: `DAY 281 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE ROPE AND THE SNAKE.`

howItsDone: Advaita Vedanta is taught in monasteries associated with Shankara, such as Sringeri, and by many modern teachers; students study the Upanishads, the Gita and the Brahma Sutras with Shankara's commentaries and contemplate the non-difference of the self and Brahman.

what a scholar hears: Shvetaketu's return and his father's question are Chandogya 6.1.1–3; the clay example is 6.1.4; 'one without a second' is 6.2.1 (ekam evādvitīyam); Advaita as a school predates Shankara (Gaudapada's Karika), and his dates are debated (traditionally 788–820).
